transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Lately I keep forgetting everyday things I’m supposed to do, like taking my pills or bringing what I need to church events, even when I write them down. It’s become quite embarrassing for me, so my primary care doctor recommended I come in for this evaluation to see what might be going on.
Have you noticed any changes in your mood, such as feeling sad, anxious, or irritable, in addition to your memory problems?

I haven't really noticed any significant changes in my overall mood like sadness or anxiety. I do occasionally feel a bit frustrated or jittery when I have to sit still or wait for things, but otherwise my mood is generally fine.
Can you tell me more about how long you've been experiencing these memory problems and if they seem to be getting worse over time?

These problems have been steadily getting worse for about two years now. It really started becoming a major issue after my husband passed away and I retired from my job. Once my days became more unstructured, I found it increasingly difficult to keep track of all my responsibilities.
Have you experienced any difficulties with learning new information, following instructions, or making decisions, in addition to the memory problems you've described?

Yes, I really struggle with following through; I'll start planning a church event but get distracted by laundry or a phone call and leave it half-done. I also find my mind drifting when trying to read committee notes or follow a Bible study, so I miss a lot of that new information. Making decisions is fine, but staying focused to finish what I start is where I have trouble.

Can you describe how you feel about your husband's passing and your retirement, and if you've been having any thoughts or feelings that might be contributing to your difficulties with focus and memory?

While losing my husband and retiring were huge adjustments, I don't feel depressed or overwhelmed by grief. The real issue is that those changes left me with a completely unstructured schedule, and I ended up taking on too many volunteer projects to fill my time. Without a set daily routine, it has become incredibly difficult to keep track of everything, which is why I'm struggling so much with my focus.
Can you think of any times or situations where your memory and focus seem to be better, such as when you're doing something you enjoy or when you have a very structured schedule?

Yes, definitely. When I was working as a senior center coordinator, having a structured schedule helped me stay much more organized and reliable. Now, even with activities I truly enjoy like gardening or quilting, I still find my mind drifting off and getting distracted because my days are so unstructured.
Have you experienced any significant loss of interest in activities that you used to enjoy, such as gardening or quilting, or has your lack of focus been the main issue?

Oh, I haven't lost interest at all; I still very much want to stay active with my gardening and quilting. The main issue is definitely my lack of focus and getting distracted, which makes it hard to follow through on these projects. I still have the drive to do them, but I just keep getting sidetracked and forgetting what I need.
Have you noticed any difficulties with language, such as finding the right words or following conversations, in addition to your memory and focus issues?

I don't have any trouble finding the right words. But I definitely struggle to follow conversations because my mind will drift off after a few minutes, and I'll realize I've missed half of what the other person was saying.
Can you describe any difficulties you've experienced with performing daily tasks that require planning or problem-solving, such as managing your finances or preparing meals?

I haven't really had much trouble with managing my finances or cooking meals specifically. However, I do tend to get very sidetracked when I'm trying to plan or organize other things, like my volunteer projects or church events.

You've mentioned that your memory and focus issues started after significant life changes, but you don't feel depressed or overwhelmed by grief. Can you tell me if you've experienced any periods of persistent sadness or loss of pleasure in activities that you normally enjoy, even if it's not a major issue for you now?

No, I really haven't experienced any persistent sadness or lost pleasure in the things I love to do. My main struggle has just been the deep frustration of trying to keep up with all my commitments and feeling like I'm constantly falling short. I still want to do everything, I just can't seem to stay on top of it all.

Can you tell me if you've noticed any difficulties with recalling recent events, learning new skills, or recognizing familiar people or places, which might help clarify what's going on with your memory and focus?

No, I don't have any trouble recognizing familiar people or places, learning new skills, or recalling past events. My forgetfulness is strictly about keeping track of my daily routines and tasks, like remembering to take my pills or bringing what I need to my meetings. It's not that I'm losing my memory of the past or getting disoriented; I just can't seem to keep my day-to-day schedule straight.

Can you rate your overall motivation to participate in daily activities and social events, despite your struggles with focus and memory, to help me understand if there's an underlying issue with motivation or if it's purely a cognitive challenge?

My motivation is actually very high, and I'm constantly on the go, bouncing from one volunteer project, church activity, or family task to the next. I genuinely want to do all of these things and have a hard time just sitting still, so it's not a lack of motivation at all. It is purely a struggle with keeping track of everything, staying focused, and organizing my unstructured time.

Can you think of any situations where you feel completely focused and able to remember everything you need to, without any distractions or memory lapses, and if so, what's different about those situations compared to your daily struggles?

I honestly can't think of any situations lately where I feel completely focused or free from these memory lapses. These struggles seem to spill into almost everything I try to do nowadays, leaving me feeling constantly scattered. I just can't seem to find any "zone" of perfect focus anymore, no matter what I'm doing.
Can you think of any times when you've felt a strong sense of purpose or engagement in an activity, and if so, did your memory and focus improve during those times?

Even when I am deeply passionate and engaged in my volunteer work or church projects, I still seem to struggle with these memory lapses and focus issues. I'm not entirely sure if my focus gets any better just because I feel a strong sense of purpose. It seems like the forgetfulness and drifting mind happen regardless of how much the project means to me.

Have you noticed any difficulties with self-monitoring, such as checking your work for errors or keeping track of your progress on tasks, which might be related to your struggles with focus and memory?

Yes, I really struggle with that; when filling out volunteer paperwork, I'll skim through and think I've done it perfectly, only for someone to point out I skipped whole sections or wrote the wrong dates. I also can't seem to track my progress because I'll start planning a church outreach, get distracted by chores or a phone call, and just wander off without finishing.
Can you describe if you've experienced any decline in your ability to perform tasks that require complex thinking, problem-solving, or judgment, compared to your past abilities?

I haven't really noticed any decline in my actual ability to think deeply, solve problems, or make decisions. My struggles are purely about staying focused, keeping track of details, and remembering to do things.
Can you tell me if you've experienced any episodes of sudden, brief periods of confusion or disorientation, which might help differentiate between potential cognitive issues?

No, I have never experienced any sudden periods of confusion or disorientation. My difficulties are strictly about forgetting my tasks, getting distracted, or losing track of what I'm supposed to do, rather than feeling confused about where I am.

Have you experienced any difficulties with word-finding, understanding written or spoken language, or with motor functions such as walking or using your hands, which could help clarify the nature of your cognitive issues?

No, I haven't experienced any of those difficulties; I don't have trouble finding words, understanding language, or with physical skills like walking or using my hands. The only things I notice are that I tend to fidget a lot when I'm sitting, and sometimes my mind drifts so I lose track of what people are saying. Otherwise, my physical and basic language abilities are completely fine.
You mentioned feeling jittery when you have to sit still and that you tend to fidget a lot; can you tell me more about how often this happens and if it's interfering with your daily activities?

It happens quite often, especially when I have to sit still for a long time, like during church sermons or council meetings. I constantly tap my foot, fiddle with my keys, or rearrange papers because of a pent-up, jittery feeling inside that makes me feel like I just have to get up and move. This restlessness makes it incredibly hard for me to pay attention and stay present during these important activities.
Can you describe how often you experience this jittery feeling and fidgeting, and if it's always present or if there are specific times or situations when it's more pronounced?

It’s not always present, but it becomes much more pronounced when I am forced to sit still for a long time, like during a long church sermon or a council meeting. In those situations, I get this pent-up, jittery sensation inside that makes me feel like I just have to get up and move. To cope with that feeling, I find myself constantly tapping my foot, fiddling with my keys, or rearranging the papers in front of me.
Have you ever been diagnosed with or experienced symptoms of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) in the past, and if so, how have those symptoms impacted your daily life?

I have never been formally diagnosed, but looking back, I definitely struggled with these symptoms as a child; my grade school report cards often said I daydreamed too much, forgot my homework, and talked out of turn. These issues have really started getting in the way over the last two years since my husband passed and I retired, to the point where people at church have stopped relying on me for important tasks. Even my daughter has started double-checking my plans because she worries I'll drop the ball with my grandkids' schedules.
Can you tell me if you have difficulty sustaining focus during tasks that you find enjoyable or interesting, or if your mind tends to wander only during tasks that you find boring or unengaging?

Yes, this difficulty happens even with tasks I genuinely care about and enjoy, like reading my garden committee notes, preparing for church outreach, or following a Bible study. My mind will still drift off or I'll get distracted and wander away to do other things, even when I really want to stay focused on these meaningful projects.
Can you describe how often you experience impulsivity, such as interrupting others, blurting out answers, or intruding on conversations, and how this affects your daily interactions?

I've definitely noticed that I frequently interrupt my kids or fellow volunteers by jumping in with my own ideas or finishing their sentences before they can finish. Sometimes I'll even start giving unsolicited advice on their projects, only to realize afterward that I've stepped on their toes. It is quite embarrassing and makes me worry about how it affects our interactions.

Can you tell me more about how your impulsivity, such as interrupting others or blurting out answers, has impacted your relationships with family and friends, and if you've noticed any changes in how they respond to you?

It has definitely caused some awkwardness and mild tension in my relationships with my kids and the other volunteers. I frequently jump in with my own ideas, finish their sentences, or offer unsolicited advice before they can even finish speaking. I usually realize afterward that I've stepped on their toes, and I can tell it makes them a bit frustrated or hesitant to share things with me.

Can you think of any times when your impulsivity, such as interrupting others or blurting out answers, has led to significant problems or conflicts in your personal or social life, and how you've handled those situations?

While it hasn't caused any major fights, I frequently interrupt my children and fellow volunteers, finish their sentences, or offer unsolicited advice on their projects. I usually realize right afterward that I've stepped on their toes, which makes me feel terribly embarrassed. Whenever I catch myself doing it, I try to apologize immediately and make sure I let them finish what they were saying.
Can you describe how often you experience restlessness or fidgeting in your daily life, and how it affects your ability to focus on tasks?

I feel restless and fidgety very frequently, especially when I am required to sit still for a long time during church sermons or council meetings. It builds up as a pent-up, jittery sensation inside, causing me to constantly tap my foot, fiddle with my keys, or rearrange papers. This restlessness makes it incredibly hard to focus on quiet tasks, so I quickly get antsy and feel compelled to either reach for a distraction or constantly bounce from one physical chore to the next.
Can you estimate how often you exhibit impulsive behaviors, such as interrupting others or blurting out answers, on a daily basis, and do you think this has increased over the past two years?

I don't have an exact daily count, but it happens regularly during conversations where I'll jump in, finish people's sentences, or give unasked-for suggestions to my kids and fellow volunteers. This behavior has definitely become much more noticeable and problematic over the past two years, ever since my life lost its structure after my retirement and my husband's passing.

Can you tell me if you have more difficulty with remembering things you need to do, like appointments or tasks, or with paying attention to details and making careless mistakes in your daily activities?

Honestly, both are major struggles for me. When it comes to remembering tasks, I regularly forget to take my vitamins, return phone calls, or bring my supplies to quilting meetings despite having lists. As for careless mistakes, I often find myself skimming through volunteer paperwork and completely skipping whole sections or writing down the wrong dates.

Can you compare how often you experience difficulties with focus and memory, such as forgetting tasks or getting distracted, versus how often you experience symptoms of restlessness, fidgeting, or impulsivity, like interrupting others or blurting out answers?

I experience both types of difficulties very frequently on a daily basis, but they affect me in different ways. The forgetfulness and focus issues, like forgetting my pills, getting distracted, or drifting off, feel much more disruptive to my daily planning and are what ultimately drove me to seek help. At the same time, the physical restlessness, constantly tapping my foot, and my tendency to interrupt others are also constant, daily habits that I catch myself doing all the time.
Can you estimate how often you feel the urge to get up and move around when you're in a situation where you're supposed to be still, such as in a meeting or during a quiet activity?

It happens almost every single time I have to sit still for more than a few minutes. During events like church council meetings or quiet activities, I quickly get a pent-up, jittery feeling inside that makes me feel like I absolutely have to get up and move around or find something to do with my hands.
